groups.name: Limits of mechanical reasoning and originality
Nature of logical thought and self-control
Historical context of logical machines and satire

sentences.text: Peirce distinguishes between "thinking" as a living process and "thought" as the product, noting that a logical machine or printed sentence embodies thought but does no thinking because it lacks life [2].
He agrees with Herbart that a thought is not the act of thinking itself, but what that act brings before the mind [3, 26].

Peirce argues that logical machines perform reasoning by working on simple principles in complex ways, and that any apparatus used for experimentation, such as a steam engine or hydrodynamic model, functions as a logical machine [23, 27, 33].
He asserts that these machines solve problems that have baffled mathematicians and that their inferences are subject to the rules of logic, even if they lack souls [1, 40, 45].
He notes that among logical machines, those expressly designed as such are often the feeblest compared to natural phenomena like hydrodynamics [4, 29].
Peirce states that a machine cannot perform even the simplest inference until premises are prepared by human observation and that it lacks originality or initiative to find its own problems [13, 27].
He argues that deductive reasoning requires an act of choice or arbitrary determination which a machine cannot perform except within narrow limits predetermined in its construction [46].
Peirce questions whether mind can be defined in terms of mechanics by asking if the mind will do something a machine cannot do [5, 25].

He illustrates this with the example of a man being roused to energetic muscular work by a faint whisper, noting that there is no relation between the mechanical energy of the whisper and the resulting contractions [5, 25].
Peirce defines logical thought as thought that is self-controlled, paralleling moral conduct [11].
He describes the elements of every concept as entering logical thought at the gate of perception and exiting at the gate of purposive action [39].
Peirce references Dean Swift's satire in "Voyage to Laputa" regarding a machine for writing books, noting that Swift's fun hit the object of satire squarely [8, 29, 41].

He mentions that logical machines were constructed in the previous decades and that Marquand's machine facilitates the treatment of problems, showing that formal logic is a small part of the mind's function in thinking [8, 24, 34].
